claims.text: High-temperature stability of high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by competition between configurational entropy and the enthalpic drive for local chemical ordering.
Compressive stress activates atomic clustering and short-range ordering.
Thermal agitation near melting activates atomic clustering and short-range ordering.
Specific pairwise interactions are responsible for clustering and short-range ordering.
Tailored molecular-dynamics potentials can capture pair probabilities, high-temperature short-range ordering, and compression-induced rearrangements in a high-entropy alloy.
A clustering-to-ordering transition stabilizes a nanoalloy against further structural degradation.
The initial nanoalloy is homogeneous and near-random at ambient conditions.
Short-range chemical order and clusters emerge from non-random interactions among constituent elements.
At high temperature, thermal energy reduces the dominance of configurational entropy.
Enthalpic contributions from favorable pair interactions trigger local atomic clustering.
Compressive loading enhances the pair interactions that produce a clustering-to-ordering transition.
Under high temperature and compression, pair-probability peaks and cluster formation will increase relative to an unstressed high-temperature baseline.
Increased local ordering and clustering correlate with enhanced resistance to structural degradation.
Tensile loading or absence of applied stress produces fewer ordering signatures than compressive loading.
Without compressive stress at high temperature, configurational entropy keeps the atomic arrangement comparatively random.
The prediction applies broadly to similar high-entropy nanoalloy compositions near melting and at moderate compressive strains.
The onset temperature and critical compressive strain depend on alloy composition and the chosen interatomic potential.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says high temperature reduces the dominance of configurational entropy, whereas the baseline says configurational entropy remains dominant at high temperature and keeps the alloy comparatively random.
